questions.q: Why does Kubernetes need the NVIDIA device plugin to schedule GPU workloads?
options: Kubernetes has no native concept of a GPU as a schedulable resource without it
The device plugin is required to install Kubernetes itself
GPUs cannot run inside containers without the device plugin
The device plugin replaces kubectl entirely
questions.explain: Unlike CPU and memory, Kubernetes has no built-in understanding of GPUs. The NVIDIA device plugin discovers GPUs on a node and advertises them to Kubernetes as a schedulable extended resource.

questions.q: What is the correct way to request one GPU in a Kubernetes pod spec?
options: resources.requests.nvidia.com/gpu: 1 only
resources.limits.nvidia.com/gpu: 1
A dedicated 'gpu:' field at the top level of the pod spec
An annotation named kubernetes.io/gpu-count
questions.explain: GPUs are requested under resources.limits.nvidia.com/gpu. For this extended resource, the limit IS the request, since a whole GPU cannot be subdivided like CPU time.

questions.q: What happens to a pod that requests a GPU when no node in the cluster currently has one available?
options: The pod runs anyway, falling back to CPU execution
The pod is automatically rejected and deleted
The pod stays in Pending status indefinitely until a GPU becomes available
Kubernetes automatically provisions a new GPU node
questions.explain: Kubernetes treats nvidia.com/gpu as a hard resource requirement. If no node can satisfy it, the pod remains Pending rather than running degraded or without a GPU.

questions.q: Under Kubernetes's resource model, what is an "extended resource"?
options: A resource that only applies to extended (long-running) jobs
A schedulable resource type beyond the built-in CPU and memory, such as nvidia.com/gpu
A deprecated resource type no longer supported
A resource that only applies to multi-node clusters
questions.explain: Extended resources are Kubernetes's mechanism for representing schedulable resources beyond the natively understood CPU and memory — GPUs advertised via the device plugin are the canonical example.

questions.q: How can you check how many GPUs a specific node has registered and how many are currently allocated?
options: kubectl get pods
kubectl describe node <node-name>, checking the Capacity and Allocatable sections
nvidia-smi run directly from the Kubernetes control plane
There is no way to check this without SSHing into the node
questions.explain: kubectl describe node shows the node's Capacity (total registered nvidia.com/gpu count) and Allocatable (how many remain unallocated to other pods).
